lessonTitle: Development of the Gut and Limbs: Midgut Rotation, Limb Buds and Oesophageal Atresia

blocks.text: A newborn is drooling heavily, coughs and turns blue at the first feed, and a feeding tube will not pass into the stomach. A tract that should be one continuous tube is closed off, and another channel leads from the airway. Understanding how the early foregut divides explains this and many other defects of the gut and of the limbs.

blocks.markdown: **The primitive gut.** During folding of the embryo in week 4, the dorsal part of the yolk sac is incorporated into the embryo as the **primitive gut tube**, lined by endoderm and surrounded by splanchnic mesoderm. It is divided into **foregut**, **midgut** and **hindgut**. Each region is supplied by a branch of the abdominal aorta: the **coeliac trunk** supplies the foregut, the **superior mesenteric artery (SMA)** supplies the midgut and the **inferior mesenteric artery** supplies the hindgut. The midgut remains connected to the yolk sac through the **vitelline duct**, which normally regresses.

blocks.title: Physiological herniation
blocks.text: Around week 6 the midgut loop elongates rapidly, and because the abdominal cavity is too small (the liver and kidneys are large) it protrudes into the umbilical cord. This normal temporary herniation is called physiological umbilical herniation. The loop returns to the abdominal cavity at about week 10.

blocks.markdown: **Rotation of the midgut.** The midgut loop has a cranial limb (future distal duodenum, jejunum and proximal ileum) and a caudal limb (distal ileum, caecum, appendix, ascending colon and proximal two thirds of the transverse colon), with the SMA as the axis. As the loop herniates it rotates **90 degrees counterclockwise** (viewed from the front), and during its return it rotates a further **180 degrees counterclockwise**, giving a total of **270 degrees**. The result is that the duodenum passes behind the SMA, the transverse colon passes in front of it, and the caecum settles in the right iliac fossa, with the ascending colon on the right and the descending colon on the left. The ascending and descending colon and parts of the duodenum then become fixed (secondarily retroperitoneal).

blocks.title: Following the rotation of the midgut
blocks.prompt: Predict the positions of the caecum and the duodenojejunal junction after a normal total rotation of 270 degrees, and describe what would happen if rotation were incomplete.

steps.text: Before rotation the midgut loop lies in the sagittal plane, with the cranial limb above and the caudal limb (with the caecal bud) below, attached to the SMA.

The loop rotates counterclockwise (viewed from the front) around the SMA. After the full 270 degrees the caudal limb has swung across in front of the SMA to the right side, so the caecum ends in the right iliac fossa with the colon framing the small bowel.
The cranial limb passes behind the SMA to the left, so the duodenojejunal flexure lies to the left of the midline.

If rotation is incomplete the caecum lies in an abnormal position (for example high in the abdomen or near the midline) and the root of the mesentery is narrow, so the bowel can twist around the SMA (midgut volvulus).

blocks.answer: Normal rotation puts the caecum in the right iliac fossa and the duodenojejunal flexure left of the midline; incomplete rotation (malrotation) leaves the caecum abnormally placed and risks midgut volvulus.

rows: Failure of the midgut to return to the abdominal cavity (failure of the body wall to close at the umbilical ring)
Bowel (often liver) in a membranous sac at the umbilicus; commonly associated with other anomalies and chromosomal abnormalities such as trisomy 18 and 13
Body wall defect, usually to the right of the umbilicus, with the cord intact; not a failure of return of physiological herniation
Bowel herniates without a covering sac; associated anomalies less common
Bilious vomiting in an infant; risk of volvulus and ischaemia
Persistence of a proximal vitelline duct remnant
Pouch on the antimesenteric border of the ileum, may contain gastric mucosa and bleed
blocks.caption: Midgut and abdominal wall anomalies.

blocks.markdown: **Limb development.** Limb buds appear at about week 4 as outgrowths of the body wall: a core of **lateral plate mesoderm** (somatic layer) covered by ectoderm. The upper limb buds appear first (about day 26-27) and the lower limb buds a couple of days later. At the distal tip of each bud the ectoderm thickens to form the **apical ectodermal ridge (AER)**, which is induced by FGF10 from the underlying mesoderm. The AER secretes fibroblast growth factors (such as FGF8) that keep the mesenchyme beneath it proliferating, driving **proximal-to-distal outgrowth** (arm, forearm, hand). The AER therefore controls limb length. A group of mesenchymal cells at the posterior border, the **zone of polarising activity (ZPA)**, secretes **Sonic hedgehog (SHH)**, which patterns the **anteroposterior axis** (thumb to little finger). Dorsal ectoderm signals (Wnt7a) pattern the dorsal-ventral axis. Hox genes help specify position and identity along the limb.

blocks.title: Role of the AER
blocks.text: The AER maintains outgrowth of the limb bud. If the AER is damaged or removed, the limb truncates at that point. Thalidomide, a teratogen taken in early pregnancy in the 1950s-60s (a historical example), caused severe reductions of the limbs (phocomelia and amelia) by disrupting limb bud development during the critical period of weeks 4-8.

blocks.markdown: **Later limb events.** At weeks 5-6 the distal ends flatten into **hand and foot plates**; digital rays form and the tissue between the rays breaks down by programmed cell death (apoptosis). Failure of this process gives **syndactyly** (webbing), and duplication of digits gives polydactyly. Limbs rotate: the upper limbs rotate 90 degrees laterally (extensor surface posterior) and the lower limbs rotate 90 degrees medially (extensor surface anterior). Long bones form by endochondral ossification from cartilage models.

**Oesophageal atresia with tracheo-oesophageal fistula (TOF).** At about week 4 a ventral groove, the laryngotracheal groove, appears in the foregut. A **tracheo-oesophageal septum** grows to separate the dorsal oesophagus from the ventral trachea. If the septum deviates posteriorly or fails to fuse completely, the oesophagus ends blindly (**oesophageal atresia**) and a connection (**fistula**) often remains between the trachea and the oesophagus. The most common form (about 85%) has a blind upper oesophageal pouch and a fistula between the trachea and the lower oesophageal segment. Oesophageal atresia prevents the fetus swallowing amniotic fluid, so it is associated with **polyhydramnios**. After birth the infant drools, chokes, coughs and becomes cyanosed with feeds, and a nasogastric tube cannot be passed. Air in the stomach on a plain radiograph indicates a distal fistula. It may be part of the VACTERL association (vertebral, anorectal, cardiac, TOF, renal and limb anomalies).

blocks.title: Reasoning from a description to a defect
blocks.prompt: A fetal ultrasound shows polyhydramnios and a small or absent stomach bubble. A neonate has a short, blind-ending oesophageal pouch but there is no air in the abdomen on radiograph. Name the defect and explain the findings.

steps.text: Polyhydramnios implies impaired swallowing of amniotic fluid, consistent with oesophageal atresia.
Absence of gas in the bowel and stomach indicates that air cannot reach the stomach from the trachea, so there is no distal tracheo-oesophageal fistula (isolated oesophageal atresia).
Embryologically, the tracheo-oesophageal septum has separated the tubes, but the oesophagus has failed to canalise or develop continuously, leaving a blind pouch.

blocks.answer: Isolated oesophageal atresia without a fistula, explaining polyhydramnios, a small stomach bubble and a gasless abdomen.

items: Midgut herniates at week 6 and returns at week 10, rotating a total of 270 degrees counterclockwise about the SMA.
Omphalocele is failure of return, covered by a sac; gastroschisis is a lateral body wall defect with no sac.
AER (FGF8) maintains outgrowth; ZPA (SHH) patterns anteroposterior axis.
Oesophageal atresia with TOF follows incomplete separation of trachea and oesophagus; polyhydramnios and drooling.

points: The midgut herniates physiologically at about week 6 and returns by week 10, rotating 270 degrees counterclockwise; failure of return gives omphalocele and incomplete rotation gives malrotation.
Limb buds form at week 4; the apical ectodermal ridge (FGF8) drives proximal-distal outgrowth and the zone of polarising activity (SHH) patterns the anteroposterior axis.
Oesophageal atresia with tracheo-oesophageal fistula results from abnormal separation of the foregut into trachea and oesophagus and presents with polyhydramnios, drooling and choking.

questions.stem: Which artery is the axis around which the midgut loop rotates?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: the SMA supplies the midgut and forms the axis of rotation.
distractorRationale.b: The coeliac trunk supplies the foregut.
distractorRationale.d: The umbilical arteries carry blood to the placenta.

questions.explanation: The midgut loop is supplied by the SMA, which runs in the mesentery of the loop and forms the axis around which it rotates 270 degrees counterclockwise.

questions.stem: A newborn has a central umbilical defect with bowel and part of the liver covered by a translucent membrane. The cord inserts onto the sac. What is the embryological explanation?

options.text: Failure of the physiologically herniated midgut to return to the abdominal cavity
Rupture of the abdominal wall to the right of a normal umbilicus
Failure of the tracheo-oesophageal septum to form

questions.correctOptionText: Failure of the physiologically herniated midgut to return to the abdominal cavity

distractorRationale.b: A defect lateral to the umbilicus without a sac is gastroschisis.
distractorRationale.c: A persistent vitelline duct gives a Meckel diverticulum or fistula, not a sac with liver.
distractorRationale.d: This describes oesophageal atresia, not a body wall defect.

questions.explanation: A central, sac-covered defect at the umbilicus containing viscera, with the cord attached to the sac, is an omphalocele due to failure of the herniated midgut to return. Gastroschisis has no sac and is lateral to the cord.

questions.stem: In experiments on a developing limb bud, the apical ectodermal ridge is surgically removed at an early stage. What is the most likely result?

options.text: The limb is truncated, with loss of distal structures
The limb develops an extra anteroposterior axis
The digits fuse but all segments are present

questions.correctOptionText: The limb is truncated, with loss of distal structures

distractorRationale.a: Correct: the AER maintains proximal-distal outgrowth.
distractorRationale.b: The anteroposterior axis is specified by the ZPA and SHH.
distractorRationale.c: Syndactyly arises from failure of interdigital apoptosis, not from AER loss.

questions.explanation: FGFs from the AER sustain proliferation of the mesenchyme at the distal tip, driving proximal-to-distal growth. Removal of the ridge stops outgrowth and truncates the limb at that level.

questions.stem: Which signalling centre specifies the anteroposterior (thumb to little finger) axis of the limb?

options.text: Zone of polarising activity secreting Sonic hedgehog

questions.correctOptionText: Zone of polarising activity secreting Sonic hedgehog

distractorRationale.a: Correct: the ZPA at the posterior margin patterns the anteroposterior axis via SHH.
distractorRationale.d: The notochord induces the neural plate and does not pattern the limb axes.

questions.explanation: Cells in the ZPA at the posterior margin of the limb bud secrete Sonic hedgehog, creating a gradient that patterns digit identity along the anteroposterior axis. The AER and dorsal ectoderm control the other two axes.

questions.stem: A fetus has polyhydramnios and no visible stomach bubble on ultrasound. Which foregut abnormality is most consistent?

options.text: Oesophageal atresia without a distal fistula

questions.correctOptionText: Oesophageal atresia without a distal fistula

distractorRationale.a: Correct: fluid cannot reach the stomach, so there is polyhydramnios and no stomach bubble.
distractorRationale.b: An H-type fistula has a patent oesophagus, so fluid is swallowed and a stomach bubble is seen.
distractorRationale.c: Gastroschisis is a body wall defect and does not typically abolish the stomach bubble or cause such polyhydramnios.

questions.explanation: If the oesophagus is blocked and there is no distal fistula, amniotic fluid cannot reach the stomach, so the stomach bubble is absent and fluid accumulates (polyhydramnios). A patent oesophagus allows swallowing.

questions.stem: An infant is found to have the following: a blind-ending upper oesophageal pouch, a fistula between the trachea and the lower oesophagus and air in the stomach on radiograph. Which embryological event failed?

options.text: Complete separation of the foregut into trachea and oesophagus by the tracheo-oesophageal septum
Rotation of the midgut around the superior mesenteric artery
Return of the herniated midgut to the abdomen

questions.correctOptionText: Complete separation of the foregut into trachea and oesophagus by the tracheo-oesophageal septum

distractorRationale.a: Correct: abnormal septation causes atresia with TOF.
distractorRationale.b: Midgut rotation concerns the intestine, not the oesophagus.
distractorRationale.c: Vitelline duct regression concerns Meckel diverticulum.
distractorRationale.d: Return of the midgut concerns omphalocele.

questions.explanation: The laryngotracheal groove is separated from the oesophagus by a tracheo-oesophageal septum. Abnormal posterior deviation of this septum leaves a blind oesophagus and a connection to the trachea, allowing air into the stomach through the fistula.

questions.stem: True or false: In a normal embryo the midgut returns to the abdominal cavity at about week 10 after rotating a total of 270 degrees counterclockwise.
questions.explanation: The midgut herniates at about week 6, rotating 90 degrees, and returns by about week 10 after a further 180 degrees, giving 270 degrees counterclockwise in total about the SMA.

questions.stem: Describe physiological herniation and rotation of the midgut, and explain how failure of return differs from incomplete rotation clinically.
markingGuide: Midgut elongates and herniates into the umbilical cord at about week 6 because the abdominal cavity is too small.
It rotates 90 degrees counterclockwise during herniation and a further 180 degrees on return at about week 10 (total 270 degrees) about the SMA.
Failure of return gives omphalocele: bowel (and liver) in a membrane-covered sac at the umbilicus, frequently with other anomalies.
Incomplete rotation (malrotation) places bowel abnormally and can cause volvulus with bilious vomiting.
Gastroschisis is a lateral body wall defect without sac, distinct from omphalocele.
questions.explanation: Herniation and rotation are normal; failure of return and failure of rotation give distinct anomalies, an omphalocele and malrotation respectively.

questions.stem: Outline the formation of a limb bud and explain the roles of the apical ectodermal ridge and the zone of polarising activity. Give one example of a teratogen that affects limb development.
markingGuide: Limb buds arise at about week 4 from lateral plate mesoderm covered by ectoderm.
AER forms at the distal ectoderm, induced by FGF10, and secretes FGF8, maintaining proliferation for proximal-distal outgrowth.
ZPA at the posterior margin secretes Sonic hedgehog to pattern the anteroposterior axis.
Hand plate, digital rays and apoptosis between digits; failure causes syndactyly.
Teratogen example: thalidomide causing phocomelia or amelia.
questions.explanation: The limb forms from mesoderm and ectoderm under the control of signalling centres. Disruption during weeks 4-8 by teratogens like thalidomide produces limb reduction defects.

questions.stem: Explain the embryological basis of oesophageal atresia with tracheo-oesophageal fistula and describe how it presents antenatally and after birth.
markingGuide: Laryngotracheal groove forms in the ventral foregut in week 4; the tracheo-oesophageal septum separates the trachea from the oesophagus.
Deviation of the septum or incomplete fusion produces oesophageal atresia with fistula.
Commonest form: blind upper pouch with a fistula from the trachea to the lower oesophagus.
Antenatal: polyhydramnios because the fetus cannot swallow amniotic fluid.
After birth: drooling, choking and cyanosis with feeding; nasogastric tube cannot be passed; air in the stomach if there is a distal fistula; association with VACTERL anomalies.
questions.explanation: Abnormal septation of the foregut leaves a blind oesophagus with a trachea-oesophageal connection. The clinical findings follow from inability to swallow and from aspiration.
